title: Pascal's Hexagon Theorem: Wiedijk #28
content: **Pascal's Theorem (1639)**: If hexagon $ABCDEF$ is inscribed in a conic section, then the three pairs of opposite sides meet in **collinear** points: $P = AB \cap DE$, $Q = BC \cap EF$, $R = CD \cap FA$. The line $PQR$ is called the **Pascal line**. Blaise Pascal discovered this at age 16, calling it the 'Hexagrammum Mysticum' (Mystic Hexagram). It is the projective dual of Brianchon's theorem (1806).
mathContext: The formalization uses projective coordinates in $\mathbb{R}^3$: points and lines are nonzero vectors, the line through $p, q$ is $p \times q$ (cross product), and collinearity is characterized by $\det(P, Q, R) = 0$. A conic is a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix $C$ with $p^T C p = 0$ defining the conic locus. The key axiom `conic_implies_pascal_constraint` encodes the Cayley-Bacharach theorem argument.

title: Projective Points and Lines
content: A `ProjPoint` is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$ (nonzero, representing a point up to scalar multiple). A `ProjLine` is also a vector in $\mathbb{R}^3$. A point $p$ lies on line $l$ iff $p \cdot l = \sum_i p_i l_i = 0$. This duality between points and lines is a hallmark of projective geometry.
mathContext: In the real projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$, a point is an equivalence class $[x:y:z]$ of nonzero vectors in $\mathbb{R}^3$ under scalar multiplication. The `valid` predicate $p \neq 0$ ensures we have a genuine projective point. The dot-product incidence condition $p \cdot l = 0$ captures the fundamental point-line duality: every statement about points and lines has a dual statement obtained by interchanging the roles of points and lines.

title: Fundamental Operations: Cross Product and Collinearity
content: The **cross product** serves double duty: `lineThrough p q = p × q` gives the line through two points, and `lineIntersection l m = l × m` gives the intersection of two lines. Three points $p, q, r$ are `collinear` iff $\det(p, q, r) = 0$ (their coordinate matrix has zero determinant). Dually, three lines are `concurrent` iff the same determinant condition holds.
mathContext: The cross product $p \times q$ is perpendicular to both $p$ and $q$, so any point on the line through $p, q$ satisfies $(p \times q) \cdot r = 0$. The identity $\det(p, q, r) = (p \times q) \cdot r$ connects collinearity to the vanishing determinant. The function `threeVectorMatrix` constructs the $3 \times 3$ matrix with rows $u, v, w$, and `Matrix.det` computes its determinant via the Leibniz formula.

title: Conic Sections in Projective Coordinates
content: A `Conic` is a symmetric $3 \times 3$ matrix $C$. A point $p$ lies on the conic iff $p^T C p = \sum_{i,j} C_{ij} p_i p_j = 0$ (the quadratic form vanishes). Non-degeneracy requires $\det(C) \neq 0$, ensuring the conic is a genuine ellipse, parabola, or hyperbola rather than a pair of lines.
mathContext: In projective coordinates, all non-degenerate conics are equivalent under projective transformations — there is no distinction between ellipses, parabolas, and hyperbolas. The quadratic form `conicQuadraticForm C p` computes $\sum_i \sum_j C_{ij} p_i p_j$. The symmetry condition $C_{ij} = C_{ji}$ ensures the conic is well-defined on projective equivalence classes (scaling $p$ by $\lambda$ scales the form by $\lambda^2$).

title: Inscribed Hexagon and Pascal Points
content: The `InscribedHexagon C` structure has six projective points $A, B, C', D, E, F$ all lying on conic $C$ (with validity conditions ensuring nonzero projective representatives). The three **Pascal points** are the intersections of opposite sides: $P = AB \cap DE$, $Q = BC' \cap EF$, $R = C'D \cap FA$, computed as cross products of line pairs.
mathContext: The structure requires $\text{pointOnConic}(A, C)$, i.e., $A^T C A = 0$ for each vertex, plus validity $A \neq 0$. The Pascal points are: $P = (A \times B) \times (D \times E)$, $Q = (B \times C') \times (E \times F)$, $R = (C' \times D) \times (F \times A)$. Pascal's theorem asserts $\det(P, Q, R) = 0$.

title: The Pascal Constraint
content: The `pascalConstraint` formalizes the algebraic condition at the heart of Pascal's theorem: for six points $A, B, C, D, E, F$, compute opposite-side intersections $P, Q, R$ via cross products, then check $\det(P, Q, R) = 0$. This is the condition that the three intersection points are collinear.
mathContext: The constraint $\det(P, Q, R) = 0$ is a polynomial identity in the coordinates of $A, \ldots, F$. When all six points lie on a conic, this polynomial vanishes identically — this is the content of the Cayley-Bacharach theorem applied to the degenerate cubics $\overline{AB} \cup \overline{CD} \cup \overline{EF}$ and $\overline{BC} \cup \overline{DE} \cup \overline{FA}$.

title: Pascal's Hexagon Theorem
content: **Pascal's Theorem** (Wiedijk #28): For hexagon $ABCDEF$ inscribed in conic $C$, the points $P = AB \cap DE$, $Q = BC \cap EF$, $R = CD \cap FA$ are collinear. The proof unfolds the definitions of `collinear`, `pascalP/Q/R`, and applies the axiom `conic_implies_pascal_constraint` which captures the Cayley-Bacharach / Bezout theorem argument.
mathContext: The axiom `conic_implies_pascal_constraint` encodes: two degenerate cubics $\Gamma_1 = \overline{AB} \cup \overline{CD} \cup \overline{EF}$ and $\Gamma_2 = \overline{BC} \cup \overline{DE} \cup \overline{FA}$ intersect in 9 points (by Bezout's theorem, $3 \times 3 = 9$). Six of these are the vertices $A, \ldots, F$ on the conic. By Cayley-Bacharach, the remaining 3 points $P, Q, R$ are collinear.

title: Special Case: Pappus's Theorem
content: When the conic degenerates to a pair of lines $l_1 \cup l_2$, Pascal's theorem specializes to **Pappus's theorem** (c. 340 AD): if $A, C, E \in l_1$ and $B, D, F \in l_2$, then $P = AB \cap DE$, $Q = BC \cap EF$, $R = CD \cap FA$ are collinear. The `collinearOnLine` predicate formalizes three points lying on a common projective line.
mathContext: Pappus's theorem is equivalent to the commutativity of the coordinate field — it holds in $\mathbb{RP}^2$ (over $\mathbb{R}$) but fails in projective planes over non-commutative division rings. This makes it one of the deepest results in the foundations of projective geometry, connecting algebra and geometry.

title: Dual: Brianchon's Theorem
content: **Brianchon's Theorem** (1806) is the projective dual of Pascal's theorem: if a hexagon is **circumscribed** about a conic (each side tangent to the conic), then the three main diagonals $AD$, $BE$, $CF$ are **concurrent**. The formalization defines the three diagonal lines via `lineThrough` and `hexagonDiagonal1/2/3`.
mathContext: Projective duality exchanges points $\leftrightarrow$ lines, collinear $\leftrightarrow$ concurrent, and inscribed $\leftrightarrow$ circumscribed. Charles-Julien Brianchon discovered this theorem in 1806 as a student at the Ecole Polytechnique, unaware it was the dual of Pascal's result from 167 years earlier. The dual formulation would assert `concurrent (hexagonDiagonal1 hex) (hexagonDiagonal2 hex) (hexagonDiagonal3 hex)`.

title: 60 Pascal Lines and the Hexagrammum Mysticum
content: Given 6 points on a conic, there are $6!/(2 \cdot 6) = 60$ distinct hexagon orderings (permutations modulo dihedral symmetry), yielding **60 Pascal lines**. These lines form a remarkable configuration with 20 **Steiner points** (each the intersection of 3 Pascal lines), 60 **Kirkman points** (each on 3 Pascal lines), and 15 **Plucker lines** (each containing 4 points). This is one of the richest incidence configurations in classical geometry.
mathContext: The 60 Pascal lines, together with the Steiner, Kirkman, and Cayley-Salmon points, form the **Hexagrammum Mysticum** configuration. Its study occupied mathematicians including Steiner (1828), Kirkman (1849), Cayley (1849), and Salmon (1852). The full configuration has $60 + 20 + 60 + 15 = 155$ geometric elements with intricate incidence relations that can be understood through the combinatorics of $S_6$.
